sections.h2: Who mails the bill and who sets the value
sections.html:
East Hampton's Receiver of Taxes prepares and mails the bills, and the town Assessor's Office decides the assessed values they rest on. The receiver's office handles over 24,000 bills a year, and each one funds Suffolk County, the town's general fund and a stack of special districts: fire, school, library, lighting, road improvement, water connection and others.

Because each parcel sits in its own combination of those districts, two houses on neighboring streets can have different totals. The town stretches from Montauk to Wainscott and includes the village of East Hampton and part of Sag Harbor. The Assessor produces the yearly roll, holds ownership and exemption files, and keeps district maps that follow the Suffolk County tax maps. Anyone can view and print a bill from the town's Tax Receiver page, even once collection has closed.

sections.h2: Payment dates and what changes after May 31
sections.html:
At town hall the season opens December 1 and closes May 31. Bills can be paid in two halves and are mailed by mid-December. Pay the first half by January 10 to avoid interest; after that 1% accrues monthly. The second half costs nothing extra until May ends.

On June 1 collection ends. The online and phone systems close, and payments move to the Suffolk County Comptroller, 330 Center Drive, Riverhead, NY 11901, telephone 631-852-3000. Put your tax map number and contact details on the payment, and send it certified if you mail it, so you have proof.

  • Late payments after May 31 draw a 5% penalty and 1% monthly interest counted from February 1, charged on tax plus penalty.
  • A tax sale advertising fee is added to anything unpaid on August 31.
  • The Comptroller takes partial payments of $200 or more, and charges penalty and interest only on the remaining balance.
  • The postmark date counts for mail, but a metered postmark does not.

An undelivered bill does not excuse the owner. Penalties and interest still apply, so request a duplicate from the receiver the moment you realize yours has not come.

Grievance season begins May 1 and ends on Grievance Day, the third Tuesday in May, which in 2027 is May 18. The complaint goes on form RP-524 to the town assessor. The assessor's calendar runs on a fixed yearly cycle:

DateWhat happens
July 1 of the prior yearValuation date
March 1Taxable status date; new exemption applications and renewals are due
May 1Tentative roll opens for public viewing and the grievance period starts
July 1Final roll for the current year
30 days after the final roll closesDeadline for a Suffolk small claims assessment review (SCAR)

Grievances and exemption forms must be delivered on paper, since email and fax are turned away. Mail yours return receipt if you want proof of delivery. The town's forms page links to a guide on disputing an assessment.

About 29,400 people lived in East Hampton in 2025, and 77.8 percent of homes are occupied by owners. Median home value is $1,178,500, so even a small adjustment in assessed value moves the bill noticeably. If your assessment looks high next to recent nearby sales, a grievance may be worth the effort.

STAR is now a credit paid by check or direct deposit, which you put toward school taxes. Owners who have received the older exemption on the bill since 2015, on the same primary residence, keep it, but new homeowners cannot get it. New Basic and Enhanced STAR applicants register with the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance.

Income limits for the credit are $500,000 for Basic, and $110,750 or less for Enhanced STAR, which is for owners aged 65 and over, in the 2026-2027 school year. The credit covers school district taxes only. To qualify in a given year you must own the home and live in it as your primary residence on July 1 of that year, so a buyer closing after that date registers for the following year.

sections.h2: Selling when tax is still open
sections.html:
Whatever is owed travels with the parcel, so settle it around the time title moves. Taxes still open at the December tax lien sale lead the Comptroller to sell a lien for that year's delinquency to Suffolk County. The owner or anyone with an interest can redeem within twelve months of the sale date, or thirty-six months for a one, two or three-family residence. After that the county issues a tax deed, and a late application to redeem goes to the Department of Planning, Division of Real Estate.

  1. Print your current bill from the receiver's portal and see what is paid for the year.
  2. For anything left from an earlier year, call the Comptroller at 631-852-3000 and ask for a payoff that includes penalty and interest.
  3. Give that number to your closing attorney or title agent so the balance is cleared at the closing table.
  4. Tell the buyer to ask the receiver for a current bill, as new owners are advised to do.

For an as-is sale the payoff is just another line item at closing.

sections.h2: Questions to settle before you accept an offer
sections.html:
Before agreeing to a price, line up the tax facts a buyer will ask about. First, which half of the current bill is paid, and are any earlier years open? Second, what district charges appear on the bill, since a buyer comparing East Hampton houses will notice that two similar homes can be billed differently. Third, is any exemption or STAR benefit tied to your name, and will the buyer need to apply on their own?

Fourth, is the bill going to the right address? A stale mailing address is one way an owner ends up never seeing a bill, and the penalties still apply. Finally, decide how you want to receive the payoff figure. Getting it by email from the receiver or Comptroller gives you a record to hand to the title agent.

If you are selling because the taxes have become a burden, say so early. A cash buyer can take that into account in the offer and can close in a time frame that stops further penalties from adding up.

sections.h2: Closing timeline for a cash sale
sections.html:
A cash buyer removes lender underwriting, so the calendar depends on title work and tax payoffs. In East Hampton the practical question is which office holds the account. Before June 1 the receiver does. After that the Comptroller does, and a figure from the wrong office will not match the payoff.

Start by finding out where your account stands. If everything is current, the closing statement will show only the usual proration. If anything is open, you will need a payoff with penalty and interest, and the title agent will pay it from proceeds. Either way, written figures from the right office and a mailing address that is correct on file help the sale close without delay.

faqs.q: When is the first half of East Hampton property tax due?
faqs.a: The first half is interest-free through January 10. From January 11 the unpaid half grows by 1% a month. The second half stays interest-free until the end of May.

faqs.q: Where do I pay East Hampton tax after May 31?
faqs.a: To the Suffolk County Comptroller at 330 Center Drive, Riverhead, NY 11901, phone 631-852-3000. The town's online and phone systems close when collection ends, so write your tax map number on a certified-mail payment.

faqs.q: Will the town waive the penalty if I never received my bill?
faqs.a: No. Owners are responsible for tax on property they own, and a bill that never arrived does not erase penalties or interest. Ask the receiver for a duplicate as soon as you notice.

faqs.q: When must an East Hampton grievance be filed?
faqs.a: By Grievance Day, the third Tuesday in May, which is May 18 in 2027. Filing opens May 1 with the tentative roll, and email or fax filings are refused.

faqs.q: Can I sell my East Hampton house while the county holds a tax lien on it?
faqs.a: Yes, if the lien is settled at or before the closing. Owners can redeem within twelve months of the lien sale, or thirty-six months for a one to three family home. Get the payoff from the Comptroller and pass it to whoever runs your closing.
